findings.title: csv_rows joins fields without calling csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with a bare `",".join(...)` over the raw stringified values, while `csv_escape` — added in the same change, immediately below — exists precisely to quote values containing a comma or a quote. Any row value such as `"Smith, John"` will be emitted unquoted and will be parsed as two columns by any CSV reader, silently shifting every subsequent column on that line. Route the values through the helper, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Note that the `str()` conversion must happen before `csv_escape`, since `csv_escape` uses the `in` operator and would raise `TypeError` on an int or None.

findings.title: csv_rows writes unescaped values, bypassing csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never calls `csv_escape`, which is added in the same commit for exactly this purpose. A row value such as `Smith, Robert` or one containing a `"` produces extra or malformed fields, so whoever supplies the record content controls the column layout of the emitted report — the classic CSV field-injection pattern (and, for values beginning `=`/`+`/`-`/`@`, formula injection once the file is opened in a spreadsheet).

Fix: route each value through `csv_escape(str(r.get(c, "")))`, or drop the hand-rolled writer in favour of the stdlib `csv` module, which handles quoting and newlines correctly.

Adversary: any user whose data ends up in an exported report. What they control: the text of a field. What they get: forged columns in the downstream CSV consumer, and potentially spreadsheet formula execution on the recipient's machine.

findings.title: csv_escape does not quote values containing newlines
findings.body: The quoting condition only tests for `,` and `"`. A field containing `\n` or `\r` must also be quoted, otherwise the embedded newline terminates the record early and the remainder of the value is read as a new row. Extend the check to `if any(ch in value for ch in ',"\n\r')`, or delegate to the stdlib `csv` module which handles all of this.

findings.title: New CSV/JSON/PDF exporter functions ship with no tests
findings.body: The repository has an established pattern of testing exporter functions (test_csv.py tests csv_header). This PR adds six new public functions (csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, usable_width) with real logic — e.g. csv_escape's quoting/escaping behavior, dump_streaming's chunking boundary, margins_for's integer-division math — none of which are covered. If any of these regress (e.g. off-by-one in chunk_size, wrong escaping logic, wrong margin math) nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: dump_streaming requires a sized sequence and breaks on chunk_size=0
findings.body: Despite the name, `dump_streaming` calls `len(rows)` and slices `rows`, so passing a generator or any other iterator raises `TypeError: object of type 'generator' has no len()` — a caller reasonably assumes a "streaming" API accepts a lazy iterable. Additionally, `chunk_size=0` (or negative) makes `range(0, n, 0)` raise `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero`. Consider consuming the input with `itertools.islice` and validating `chunk_size >= 1`.

findings.title: New test doesn't test the expiry window and is time-flaky
findings.body:
`test_token_issued_today_is_valid` calls `is_expired(token.expires_at)` without passing `now`, so it depends on the real wall clock at test-run time rather than the fixed `now` values used in `test_token_expires_after_an_hour`. Unless `is_expired`'s default expiry window is broken by hours/days, this assertion will pass regardless of whether the boundary logic (the actual thing the PR title says it tests) is correct — it never exercises the near-expiry edge. It also makes the suite flaky around midnight/day boundaries via `token.issued_at.date() == datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()`. Inject an explicit `now` near the token's expiry boundary, as the sibling test does, to actually validate the expiry window.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `is_expired` called without `now=`, unlike every other call in the file

findings.title: First argument to `is_expired` may not be an expiry timestamp
findings.body: On line 6 the first positional argument is `issued + timedelta(hours=2)` against `now = issued + 1h1s` — i.e. the reference time is *before* that timestamp, yet the test asserts expiry is true. That only makes sense if the first parameter is the token's *issue* time (with a one-hour window baked in), not its expiry time. If so, passing `token.expires_at` on line 12 is feeding the wrong field and the assertion is checking something other than what it claims. Worth confirming the parameter's meaning against the implementation.

findings.title: No test covers CouponExpired rejection path
findings.body: The PR adds logic to raise CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, exercising only the non-expired branch. If the comparison were inverted, the exception were never raised, or the wrong exception type were used, no test would fail. Add a test that passes an already-expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: apply_coupon now requires expires_at; missing/None values raise, not reject
findings.body: `apply_coupon` previously only read `coupon.amount`. Line 9 makes `coupon.expires_at` mandatory: if a coupon object has no such attribute the call dies with `AttributeError`, and if the field is `None` (the natural representation of a never-expiring coupon) the comparison dies with `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`. Either way the caller sees an opaque crash rather than `CouponExpired`, and a perpetual coupon becomes unusable. The test diff on tests/test_coupons.py line 3 is direct evidence that existing construction sites did not supply `expires_at`. Guard the check, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now:`, and confirm every producer of coupon objects populates the field.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body: `fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async def` but contains no `await`; it calls the synchronous `requests.get`. Awaiting this coroutine from request handling blocks the entire event loop until billing.internal responds — up to the 5 second timeout — stalling every other concurrent request in the process, not just this one. The module already has an async HTTP path (`httpx.AsyncClient` in `fetch_plan` on line 5-7); use `await client.get(...)` with an `httpx.AsyncClient` against the billing host, or, if the sync library must be kept, move the call off the loop with `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor`.

findings.title: Async function name contradicts blocking behavior
findings.body: The function `fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but performs a synchronous blocking call via `requests.get()` on line 11. This violates the implicit contract that callers would expect from an `async` function: that it does not block the event loop. A caller using this in an async context (awaiting it) will experience blocking behavior they did not expect from the function signature. Either rename it to `fetch_plan_limits_blocking` to signal its true nature, or refactor it to use `httpx` like the existing `fetch_plan` function to honor the async contract.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. `tenant_id` is untyped and unvalidated here. If it originates from a request parameter (path segment, query string, JSON body), a caller can supply values such as `..%2f..%2fadmin/tenants` or `1/../../invoices` and address endpoints on `billing.internal` other than `/limits/<id>` — a server-side request forgery against a host that is presumably only reachable from inside the network, using this service as the proxy. The same shape already exists on line 6 for the httpx call, but this new function targets an internal-only host, which is the more valuable pivot.

Fix: validate the identifier before use (e.g. assert it matches `^[0-9a-fA-F-]+$` or coerce to `int`), and/or pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")` rather than raw interpolation. Constraining the type at the call boundary is the cheaper of the two.

findings.title: No test coverage for fetch_plan_limits' blocking call behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but calls requests.get synchronously, which blocks the event loop. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that would catch this — a test asserting only on the JSON return value, or a test using a mocked requests.get, would pass regardless of whether the call blocks the loop. Since this is the core behavior change being introduced (fetching plan limits during request handling), a test verifying non-blocking behavior (e.g. via anyio/asyncio concurrency test or ensuring it runs in a thread executor) is needed to catch this class of regression.

findings.title: Bare except swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is running are converted into a silent `return None`. That breaks shutdown/cancellation semantics for the whole process, not just the metrics path. It also swallows programming errors in `_client.send` (`TypeError`, `AttributeError`, serialization bugs in `payload`) with no trace at all — the PR description says "catch and log", but no logging happens here, so failures are completely invisible.

Narrow it to `except Exception as exc:` and emit a log record (e.g. `logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=exc)`) before returning.

findings.title: No test covers the new failure-swallowing behaviour
findings.body: push_metrics now catches all exceptions from _client.send and returns None instead of propagating, but no test exercises either the success path or the failure path. A test asserting that push_metrics returns None (and doesn't raise) when _client.send throws would catch a regression if this logic were later broken (e.g. accidentally re-raising, or catching too narrowly).

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, then yields control at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 — all without acquiring `_lock`. Any number of tasks can pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16 before any of them writes, so the tenant's counter can be driven arbitrarily above `LIMIT` and the rate limit does not actually limit. The existing `consume` on lines 8-11 already establishes the house pattern: hold `_lock` for the whole read-modify-write. Wrap the entire body of `try_consume` in `async with _lock:` (the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` inside the critical section is harmless since it never blocks on another lock holder), or drop the sleep and do the check-and-increment as a single synchronous step under the lock.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act with await in between

findings.title: try_consume's race condition and limit behavior are untested
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters and checks the limit outside the _lock, then awaits asyncio.sleep(0) before writing back — a classic check-then-act race under concurrent calls for the same tenant, which could allow the limit to be exceeded. No test in this diff exercises concurrent calls to try_consume, nor does any test verify the basic limit-enforcement behavior (rejecting when current+cost>LIMIT) or the success path. If this function were wrong (e.g. race allowed overshoot, or limit boundary off-by-one), nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of the `(name, email)` tuple. The docstring states the function returns '(name, email)' as a tuple, but line 6 returns a dict with keys 'name', 'email', and 'tier'. findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil after a failed insert
findings.body:
The `err` bound by `if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil` only exists inside that `if` statement. After logging, control falls through to `var err error` — a brand-new variable whose zero value is `nil` — and `return err` therefore always reports success. Any caller doing `if err := WriteSettlement(db, s); err != nil { ... }` will treat a dropped settlement row as a committed one, which in an end-of-day batch means silent financial data loss with no retry or reconciliation signal.

If the intent really is log-and-continue, the function should return `nil` explicitly (and preferably not advertise an `error` return, or return a sentinel the batch loop can count); if the intent is propagation, capture the error in the outer scope:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

The dead `var err error` strongly suggests the propagating version was intended.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Failed settlement insert is reported as success to the caller

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ WriteSettlement silently ignores insert failures

findings.title: No test covers WriteSettlement's error-return behavior

There is no test in this diff exercising WriteSettlement with a failing db.Exec to verify the returned error, so this always-nil-return defect would go undetected by CI.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits `attempted` shares the same list object. Line 10 appends into that shared list and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns its own failures plus all failures from the first call, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Callers that treat the return value as "the recipients that failed in this batch" will get wrong results and may re-send to recipients that already succeeded.

Use the standard sentinel form:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
```

findings.title: No test exercises mutable-default-arg bug in send_with_retries

A single test that calls it once with all-successful dispatches and checks the return value would pass regardless of this bug. Nothing in the diff catches the case of calling the function multiple times (with failures) and observing that the 'attempted' list accumulates stale entries from previous calls.

findings.title: Rounding boundary changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 inside a rename
findings.body: This PR is described as a pure rename, but `compute_rounding` also changes the comparison from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. For the exact boundary value `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1 — a one-cent difference per line item, in the direction that under-bills. Half-cent remainders are the single most common input to a rounding helper (any value ending in .5 from a half-of-odd-cents split), so this is reachable, not theoretical. If the behaviour change is intended, it belongs in its own commit with a test pinning the 0.5 case; otherwise restore `>=`.

findings.title: Rounding boundary change (>= to >) has no accompanying test
findings.body: The PR is described as a pure rename of calc_* to compute_*, but compute_rounding's comparison changed from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. This changes the return value for the exact boundary case remainder_cents == 0.5 (previously rounded up returning 1, now returns 0). findings.title: Module docstring misleads after rename to compute_*
findings.body: The module docstring says 'Line-item calculators' but the functions have been renamed from `calc_*` to `compute_*`. The new names better describe what these functions actually do: retrieve pre-calculated values from line objects (e.g., `line.subtotal_cents`). They are getters/accessors, not calculators. The docstring should be updated to reflect the new naming convention and the actual behavior of these functions.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops a record per page
findings.body:
The slice end is `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, so each page yields at most `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records. Because `start` still advances by the full `PAGE_SIZE` per page, the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — it is skipped entirely rather than deferred to the next page. For an export endpoint this means silent data loss for every tenant with more than one page. The pre-existing `page_of` on line 6 uses `records[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`, which is the correct form; change line 12 to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]` to match.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted returns one fewer item than page_of

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge_card` retries `billing.gateway.charge` up to 3 times. The gateway declares that call NOT idempotent: "each call creates a new charge". Any failure mode where the request reaches the gateway but the response is lost (timeout, connection reset, 502 from a proxy after the POST landed) will cause the retry decorator to POST again, double- or triple-charging the customer. The failure is silent — the caller sees one success.

The gateway docstring already points at the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key per logical charge attempt in `charge_card` (not per HTTP attempt) and pass it through to `charge`, so all three attempts collapse to one charge server-side. Until `charge` accepts and forwards such a key, the retry should be removed from this path rather than left on.

findings.title: Retryable wrapper on non-idempotent operation lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The new `charge_card()` function wraps `charge()`, which is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent: "each call creates a new charge." The wrapper function has no docstring explaining how retries are safe, and the underlying function's warning about requiring an Idempotency-Key header is now invisible to callers of `charge_card()`. A caller relying on the `@retry` decorator could believe retries are safe when they are not.

findings.title: No test would catch duplicate charges from retrying a non-idempotent call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge with @retry(attempts=3), but gateway.charge's docstring explicitly states it is NOT idempotent and each call creates a new charge unless an Idempotency-Key is passed. The diff adds no test verifying retry behavior here, so a test suite that already exercises fetch_charge's retry (line 5-7) would not exist for charge_card, and nothing would fail if a transient error caused charge_card to double-charge a customer on retry.

findings.title: Naive datetime subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body: `datetime.now()` returns a naive local-time datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Note that even if the tz-awareness were patched by attaching the local zone, using local wall-clock time instead of UTC would still shift the cutoff on any non-UTC host.

findings.title: Timezone-aware value compared to naive datetime
findings.body: The `expires_within()` function creates a naive `cutoff` datetime on line 9 and subtracts it from `invite.expires_at`, which is guaranteed to be timezone-aware UTC (per the Invite model's documented contract). This comparison will raise `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` at runtime. The fix is to make `cutoff` timezone-aware: `datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0)`, matching the pattern in `is_expired()` on line 5.

findings.title: expires_within has no test and mixes naive/aware datetimes untested
findings.body: expires_within is new and ships with no test at all. Given invite.expires_at is documented as always tz-aware (models/invite.py), but cutoff here is built from datetime.now() without timezone, the subtraction on line 10 would raise TypeError at runtime for any real Invite. findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding". `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it directly, so for any account that has not completed onboarding this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')` at runtime — and will fail to compile under `strictNullChecks`. Suggest mirroring the existing style, e.g. return `account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? ""` (or a sentinel/`undefined` return type that callers handle), or narrow with an explicit check before dereferencing.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body:
`fetch()` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `30` gives a 30 ms budget — shared across the default 3 retries — to an API the PR description calls slow. This will time out on essentially every nightly run, and because no exception handling is present the whole sync job will fail. If 30 seconds was intended, pass `timeout=30_000`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ timeout argument passed in seconds, not milliseconds

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering its call to fetch
findings.body: The diff adds sync_partner_catalogue() which calls fetch() with a hardcoded timeout value, but no test exercises this function. Given that fetch()'s timeout parameter has a non-obvious unit contract (milliseconds, per clients/http.py docstring) and the value passed here (30) looks like it was chosen in seconds, a test asserting the correct call (e.g. via a mock/stub with the expected timeout_ms) would catch a wrong-unit regression or any other behavioural change to this new sync path. As it stands, nothing in the repo would fail if this function's behaviour were wrong.

findings.title: Duplicate of existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body: Migration 0007 already created `invoices_tenant_created_idx ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — identical table, identical column list, identical sort direction. This new index is functionally redundant: the planner will use the existing one for the reporting query, while every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on `invoices` now pays to maintain a second copy, plus the storage and the build time of a CONCURRENTLY index on a large table. The `IF NOT EXISTS` guard gives no protection here because it matches on index *name*, and `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` != `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, so it will always create. Drop this statement; if the intent was to rename or to change the definition (e.g. add an INCLUDE column or a partial predicate), make that explicit and drop the old index in the same migration.

findings.title: priority=9 de-prioritises reset mail; the scale is inverted
findings.body:
`queue.priority.enqueue` documents priority as an ordering index where **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last** — explicitly noting it is "the opposite of what the name suggests". Passing `priority=9` therefore places password-reset email behind every other queued job, including the nightly digest batch this PR is trying to jump ahead of. It is also strictly worse than the previous behaviour, which used the default of 5.

To get the intended effect, pass `priority=0` (or a low value such as 1 if 0 is reserved for something more urgent).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ priority=9 is drained last, delaying password-reset mail

findings.title: Priority 9 queues jobs last, not first
findings.body: The code now sets priority=9 for password reset emails, but the docstring in queue/priority.py explicitly documents that priority 0 is drained first and priority 9 is drained last. A priority of 9 will cause reset emails to queue behind digests, not ahead of them. To queue resets ahead of digests, use a lower priority value (e.g., 0 or 1).

findings.title: No test would catch the inverted priority value
findings.body: send_reset_email now calls enqueue(..., priority=9), but per queue/priority.py's docstring, priority 9 means drained last, not first — the opposite of the stated goal of moving reset emails ahead of the digest batch. There is no test asserting the priority value passed to enqueue, so this behavior change (correct or, as appears likely, backwards) is unverified and would silently ship either way.

findings.title: Violates upsert() contract: terms must be lower-cased and de-duplicated
findings.body: The call to `upsert(article.id, article.title.split())` passes terms that violate the documented preconditions. According to the docstring in search/index.py, `upsert()` requires that terms be already lower-cased and de-duplicated. Passing `article.title.split()` directly will fail both requirements: title case is preserved, and any repeated words in the title create duplicates. This means articles will either index under incorrect case-sensitive terms (making them unfindable by queries) or fail silently. Either fix the terms before passing them (lower-case and de-duplicate) or update the upsert docstring to document that it performs these operations.

findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised title terms
findings.body: `upsert` documents that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, and explicitly states it performs no normalisation itself: a term differing only by case creates a separate posting list that lower-casing queries will never hit. `article.title.split()` yields the title's words verbatim, so any capitalised word — which is most words in a typical title — is indexed under a key no query can reach, and the article is silently unfindable by it. Normalise before the call, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {w.lower() for w in article.title.split()})` (and consider stripping punctuation, since `split()` leaves trailing commas/periods attached to terms).

findings.title: publish() indexing behavior is untested and violates upsert's contract
findings.body: publish() now calls upsert(article.id, article.title.split()), but article.title.split() is not lower-cased or de-duplicated, which upsert's docstring explicitly says will cause silent unfindability for terms differing only by case. No test in this diff exercises publish() to verify indexed terms are queryable, so this defect (and any future regression in how terms are prepared before indexing) would not be caught.

findings.title: Referer header logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch redacted query parameters from the `Referer` value via `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before it was put in `headers`. After this change `headers["Referer"] = request.headers["Referer"]` is stored raw and then serialised into the log line at line 6.

Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and the docstring states explicitly that the browser therefore sends the token back in the `Referer` header on every subresource request. So any 5xx triggered while a token-bearing page is open writes a live authentication token into the log stream — logs are routinely shipped, aggregated, and readable by people who are not entitled to the token, and the token grants full server access.

Restore the scrubbing for the `Referer` header (and keep passing `extra_param_keys` through), rather than dropping it. If the goal was to simplify the loop, apply `_scrub_uri` unconditionally to URL-valued headers instead of removing it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token now logged verbatim via unscrubbed Referer header

findings.title: Documentation describes token scrubbing that code no longer performs
findings.body: The diff removes the `_scrub_uri()` call that previously redacted tokens from Referer headers (line 5-6 in the original code). If the module or function documentation states that tokens are scrubbed from logged headers, or that Referer headers are sanitized, that documentation is now inaccurate. A caller or maintainer reading the docs would expect token redaction to occur, but it no longer does. Either restore the scrubbing or update the documentation to reflect that raw Referer headers—including tokens—are now logged.

findings.title: No test guards against reintroducing the unscrubbed Referer log
findings.body: The change deletes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, so the auth token embedded in Referer (per token_authenticated_url) will now be written verbatim into logs on any 5xx. There is no test in this diff exercising this logging path with a Referer header containing a token, so this regression would pass silently. Add a test that triggers the 5xx logging path with a Referer containing a token query param and asserts the token is absent/scrubbed in the emitted JSON.

findings.title: `extra_param_keys` appears to become unused after removing the scrub call

If the scrubbing is restored as recommended this resolves itself; otherwise the now-unused parameter and its callers should be cleaned up so no one assumes redaction is still happening.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from URL check re-enables SVG javascript: XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `javascript:`, `data:text/html` and `vbscript:` prefixes listed in `unsafeLinkPrefix`. After this change `xlinkhref` no longer reaches that check, so it falls through to whatever the default allow path is and is emitted to the DOM unfiltered. Adversary: any end user who can submit markdown (the file's own comment states that authored markdown "includes content submitted by end users"). What they control: the attribute value, e.g. ``. What they get: script execution in the origin of every viewer who activates the link — session cookies, tokens, and any action the viewer is authorised to take. `xlink:href` on SVG `` is honoured for `javascript:` URLs in real browsers and is a standard sanitiser-bypass vector; it is exactly why it was in the list. Restore `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` (and consider normalising `xlink:href`/`xlinkHref` spellings to the same key so the check cannot be side-stepped by casing or the colon form). _Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Dropping xlinkhref skips URL scheme validation on xlink:href

findings.title: No test exercises removal of 'xlinkhref' from validateProp
findings.body: The diff removes 'xlinkhref' from the set of attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed in validateProp. There is no accompanying test file in this PR, so if this change unintentionally allows an unsafe xlink:href value through (or breaks a legitimate use case), nothing in the test suite would fail. Add a test that calls validateProp (or the higher-level sanitiser) with attribute='xlinkhref' and a malicious value (e.g. 'javascript:...') and asserts the resulting behavior, so future changes to this list are caught.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets query param reach path join (traversal)
findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is caller-controlled data taken straight off the HTTP request. Previously every non-empty value had to pass `common.ValidateID` (an identifier format check) before the handler continued; this diff removes that gate, leaving only the equality check against `parameters.Project` on line 4 — which is skipped entirely when the path parameter is absent.

The value then reaches the file DAO, whose `buildPath` does `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and explicitly documents "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." `filepath.Join` calls `Clean`, so a project value of `../../etc` resolves outside `d.Folder`. Adversary: any client able to call the list endpoint. Controls: the `project` query string. Gets: read of documents outside the configured storage root (and, for other kinds, listing of arbitrary directories).

The PR description's premise — "the path join already scopes under the folder root" — is incorrect for `filepath.Join`, which normalises `..` rather than rejecting it. Restore the `ValidateID` call, or push equivalent validation/containment (e.g. reject separators and `..`, or verify the cleaned path is still prefixed by `d.Folder`) into `buildPath`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unvalidated project query param reaches buildPath, enabling path traversal

findings.title: Removed validation of projectQueryParameter has no regression test
findings.body: The check that called common.ValidateID on projectQueryParameter (and returned a bad-request error on failure) has been deleted, but there is no test in this diff exercising list() with a malformed or path-traversal-like project name (e.g. containing '../' or invalid characters) to confirm the new unvalidated value is safely handled downstream. Given buildPath's own documentation states it performs no validation and requires callers to validate names first, this behavior change is exactly the kind that needs a test asserting either the resulting path is still safe or that invalid input is still rejected somewhere. As it stands, nothing would fail if this change reintroduces unsafe path construction.

findings.title: Part buffer pre-allocated from client-declared Content-Length
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory up front based on a value the uploading client declares, before a single byte of `body` has been read. Previously the RW grew a page at a time as `io.Copy` consumed the body, so a part could only ever occupy as much memory as the client actually transmitted; now a request that advertises `Content-Length: 1099511627776` and then sends nothing (or trails off) costs the server that allocation immediately. Concurrent part uploads multiply it, so a handful of cheap requests can drive the process into OOM.

Fixes: clamp the reservation to a sane per-part ceiling (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartSize)`) and let the RW grow beyond that only as real bytes arrive; reject `contentLength` larger than the configured maximum part size before allocating; and guard the unknown-length case (`contentLength == -1` for chunked/streaming uploads) so it is not passed into `Reserve` at all.

Adversary: any client permitted to issue an upload-part request to `serve s3` — they control only the declared length header, and they get an unbounded server-side allocation for a request whose body they never have to send.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Reserve called with a possibly negative/unknown Content-Length

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from attacker-controlled Content-Length
findings.body:
`contentLength` on an S3 UploadPart request comes straight from the client's `Content-Length` header; nothing in the shown code bounds or validates it before it reaches `Reserve`. Previously the RW grew a page at a time as `io.Copy` actually consumed bytes, so peak memory tracked the bytes really delivered. After this change the allocation happens up front, so a request advertising e.g. `Content-Length: 5368709120` with a one-byte (or immediately aborted) body causes the server to commit that much memory before reading anything — and concurrent part uploads multiply it.

Fix by clamping the reservation to a sane ceiling (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartBuffer)`) and letting the RW grow beyond that only as bytes genuinely arrive, and/or rejecting the request when `contentLength` exceeds the configured maximum part size.

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) behavior or edge cases
findings.body: The change adds a call to Reserve(contentLength) to pre-allocate the multipart buffer. There is no test in this diff verifying that the reservation produces correct behavior, particularly for edge cases like contentLength being -1 (unknown length, common with chunked transfer encoding) or a contentLength that doesn't match the actual body size. If Reserve mishandles these cases (e.g., panics on negative size, or under/over-allocates), existing tests would not catch it since none appear to exercise this code path with varying Content-Length values.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgrades to HTTP when the caller *explicitly* sets `is_secure=False`; any other value, including a missing key (`None`), yields HTTPS. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats every falsy value the same, so `request.meta` without an `is_secure` key — the default for essentially every request — now produces `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...`. AWS credentials/signatures and object payloads would be sent unencrypted, and the URL used on line 6 changes for existing callers that never opted out of TLS.

If the goal is just to simplify, preserve the default by reading it as `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)` and keeping the truthiness test, or restore the `is False` sentinel check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 handler now defaults to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset

findings.title: Scheme default flip has no test guarding it
findings.body: The change alters the default scheme when `is_secure` is absent/unset from `https` (old code) to `http` (new code), and also changes behavior for falsy-but-not-`False` values (e.g. `None`, `0`, missing key) since the old code specifically checked `is False` while the new code uses truthiness. There is no test in this diff exercising `download_request` with `is_secure` unset, `None`, or explicitly `True`/`False` to confirm the resulting `scheme` value. If this logic were wrong (e.g., defaulting to insecure `http` unintentionally), nothing in the existing suite (not shown, and not part of this diff) would catch it.

findings.title: DELETE now authorised as "push", dropping the delete permission check
findings.body:
The removed `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch means a DELETE request now falls into the `!= GET && != HEAD` arm and is checked against the `push` action. The retrieved config documentation states explicitly that the three actions are distinct "on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones." After this change any principal holding only `push` on a repository can delete tags/manifests, and any policy that grants `delete` without `push` will now be denied. Restore the DELETE branch so `requestedAccess.Action` is `"delete"` for `http.MethodDelete`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorises as "push", bypassing the delete permission

findings.title: Unlisted methods (OPTIONS, TRACE) default to push instead of pull
findings.body: The old switch had an explicit `default: action = "pull"` for methods outside HEAD/GET/POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE. The inverted condition now sends every such method — notably `OPTIONS` (CORS preflight) — down the `push` path, so read-only or anonymous clients that previously passed the pull check will be denied. If the intent was only to simplify the mapping, keep the non-mutating methods (at minimum GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) on `pull`.

findings.title: No test guards DELETE now mapping to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The mapping change makes http.MethodDelete resolve to action 'push' instead of the previous 'delete', per repository docs distinguishing push/delete as separate authorization actions. This diff contains no test changes, so if this mapping is wrong (e.g. it should still require a distinct delete permission), nothing in the test suite would fail to catch it.

findings.title: Full cache clear at 1000 entries makes get_tenant return None for all tenants
findings.body:
When the cache crosses 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` discards every entry, not just the oldest. The existing reader `get_tenant` (line 5) is a pure `dict.get` with no fallback to `_fetch`, so immediately after any clear every `get_tenant(...)` call returns `None`. Callers cannot distinguish "not cached" from "tenant does not exist", so this silently turns a capacity event into wrong results across the whole service.

Consider a bounded eviction instead (drop a single/oldest key, or use `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache` semantics), or make `get_tenant` fall back to `_fetch` on a miss so a clear only costs latency rather than correctness.

findings.title: Caller-supplied key fills shared cache, then flushes it entirely
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` inserts an entry into the shared `_CACHE` for every `tenant_id` it is called with, including ids that do not correspond to a real tenant (whatever `_fetch` returns is stored unconditionally on line 10). When the map exceeds 1000 entries the entire cache is discarded (lines 11-12) rather than evicting the oldest entry.

If `tenant_id` is ever reachable from a request parameter, an attacker who can issue ~1000 requests with distinct ids can (a) evict every legitimately cached tenant, sending all subsequent `get_tenant` reads to a miss, and (b) repeat this cheaply to keep the cache permanently cold, amplifying load on whatever `_fetch` talks to. Note also that `get_tenant` (line 5) returns `None` on a miss rather than fetching, so a flush changes observable behaviour for other callers, not just performance.

Suggested fix: bound the cache with an LRU/size-limited structure (e.g. `functools.lru_cache` or an explicit oldest-key eviction) instead of `clear()`, and avoid caching entries for ids that `_fetch` reports as non-existent.

findings.title: A None/absent result from _fetch is cached unconditionally
findings.body: The result of `_fetch(tenant_id)` is written into `_CACHE` without checking it. If `_fetch` can return `None` (or an empty placeholder) for an unknown or temporarily unavailable tenant, that negative result is now cached and served by `get_tenant` indefinitely. Guard the write, e.g. only store when `tenant is not None`.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has no test coverage
findings.body: The new function fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared cache, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff: a bug in the cache-write, the eviction threshold, or the return value would go unnoticed. Add a test that calls get_tenant_fresh, asserts the returned tenant matches the fetched value, confirms it was stored in _CACHE, and verifies the clear-on-overflow behavior at the 1000 boundary.

findings.title: Documentation references renamed flag --workers
findings.body:
The README documents `--workers` as a command-line flag, but the code (cli.py line 6) has renamed this flag to `--concurrency`. Users following the README will encounter an unrecognized argument error. Update the README to document the correct flag name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Renaming --workers also renames args.workers, breaking callers
findings.body:
`add_argument("--concurrency", ...)` changes the parsed namespace attribute from `args.workers` to `args.concurrency`. Any code that reads `args.workers` (or builds a dict/kwargs from the namespace) will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime rather than fail at import, so it will not be caught by a smoke test of `parser()` alone. It also breaks existing command lines and scripts that pass `--workers`, which argparse will now reject with "unrecognized arguments".

If the intent is purely a user-facing rename, keep the destination stable and/or accept the old spelling: `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)`. Otherwise, grep for `\.workers` across the codebase and update every consumer in this PR.

findings.title: Renamed CLI flag has no test verifying new name or callers
findings.body: The flag `--workers` was renamed to `--concurrency`, changing both the CLI interface and the resulting attribute name (`args.workers` -> `args.concurrency`). No test file is present in the diff to confirm the parser accepts `--concurrency` or that any code consuming `args.workers` was updated. If a caller elsewhere still reads `args.workers`, it will now raise an AttributeError at runtime, and nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping day strings to counts. Callers relying on the documented contract will receive an unexpected data structure and fail. Update the docstring to describe the new return format: a dict mapping day to count.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict; callers will break silently
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns a `dict` mapping day -> count. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now either raise a `TypeError` or silently produce a wrong result (a dict is truthy whenever there is at least one day of data). findings.title: No test covers the new per-day breakdown return shape

This is a breaking API contract change (also reflected in the stale docstring on line 2). findings.title: Docstring parameter name stale after rename
findings.body:
The docstring on line 6 still documents the parameter as 'page_size', but the function signature on line 1 has renamed it to 'limit'. Callers reading the docstring will see documentation that does not match the actual parameter name they must use, causing confusion and potentially incorrect usage. Update the docstring to reflect the new parameter name.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed `page_size` parameter

findings.title: Renamed keyword parameter breaks callers using page_size=
findings.body: `page_size` was a positional-or-keyword parameter of a module-level (public-looking) function; renaming it to `limit` silently breaks any caller that passes it by keyword (`list_invoices(t, page_size=100)`) with a `TypeError`, while positional callers keep working.
